dispatch.headline: Officer Drops Wet Rope Into Space
dispatch.body:
Odile Laine cut the engines to shove forty metres of wet hemp rope into the void.

The chief maritime officer on the migrant transport Archon insisted the voyage could not begin without an unmooring.

"You cannot simply slide away," Laine said from the flight bay. "That is drifting. A ship leaves a quay."

She cited the Dover Port Act of 1547. Under the statute, any vessel entering deep water must cast off a wet line from a physical slipway.

Fleet managers told Laine to sleep on the order. She slept on the order, which was three sheets of stiff plastic.

Her deck mate, Rosalind Gallagher, held a wash bucket while Laine pushed the soaked fibres through the lock.

The rope froze solid.

It did not drift away.

In the vacuum between stations, the frozen hemp rod floated outside the bridge glass, matching speed with the transport.

Laine watched it with quiet satisfaction.

"Look at that," she said. "Proper seamanship."

Admiralty rules forbid a ship from passing its own cast line. The Archon has crept behind the rope for nine days.
dispatch.scene: A woman in a grey flight suit shoves a dripping coil of rope through an open round airlock hatch into black space, a crewmate holding a plastic bucket behind her.
dispatch.premise: The chief maritime officer aboard the migrant vessel Archon halts transit through deep space to force the crew to throw a wet hemp rope into the vacuum, citing an unrepealed 16th-century admiralty law requiring ships to cast off from a physical quay.
